title: Parity Mapping for Quantum Optimization on Frustrated Ising Rings
authors: Ruiyi Wang, Anita Weidinger, Glen Bigan Mbeng, Wolfgang Lechner, Giuseppe E. Santoro
abstract: The frustrated Ising ring is one of the simplest models exhibiting exponential closing spectral gaps, making it a paradigmatic and challenging benchmark for quantum annealing (QA). Ground-state preparation for this model has therefore been studied extensively in both continuous-time QA and digitized protocols such as the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). Here, we use the frustrated Ising ring to investigate how the parity mapping affects the performance of both QA and QAOA. For QA, finite-size calculations show that the parity mapping increases the minimum spectral gap under the energy normalization used in this work, thereby enabling faster continuous-time ground state preparation protocols. An ideal implementation of Parity-QA, with a single global constraint, shows no evidence of exponential gap closing over the accessible system sizes, whereas a hardware-motivated decomposition into local constraints restores the exponential decrease, albeit with a smaller fitted exponent than conventional QA. For the digitized protocol, we find that the number of Parity-QAOA layers required to prepare the exact ground state remains constant over the simulated sizes, improving upon the quadratic scaling required by conventional QAOA. To investigate the role of constraints in Parity-QAOA, we further consider a modified Ising ring instance in which the constraint term is essential for preparing the target ground state. We then compare the corresponding resource requirements with those of conventional QAOA.
summary: This work analyzes the use of parity mapping to enhance quantum optimization on frustrated Ising rings. By applying this technique, the authors demonstrate significant theoretical improvements for both Quantum Annealing and QAOA protocols compared to standard methods. This suggests that constraint encoding via parity qubits can lead to more robust and scalable quantum computation algorithms.
main_problem: The paper investigates how applying a 'parity mapping' technique affects the performance of quantum optimization algorithms (QA and QAOA) when solving problems on frustrated Ising rings.
main_result: Parity mapping improves both continuous-time Quantum Annealing by increasing spectral gaps and discrete QAOA by achieving constant layer scaling, outperforming conventional methods in complexity metrics.
method: The authors analyze the performance of two quantum optimization protocols—Quantum Annealing (QA) and QAOA—on a frustrated Ising ring using theoretical analysis and state-vector simulations.
model_or_system: The system is the frustrated Ising ring, modeled by a target Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{\text{target}}$. The core technique involves mapping local interactions to parity qubits via Parity Mapping, which introduces constraint Hamiltonians ($\tilde{H}_c$) into the overall problem formulation.
key_observables: Minimum spectral gap (for QA), number of required QAOA layers, and circuit complexity metrics like CNOT depth.
important_parameters: The coupling strengths ($J_j$), constraint strength ($C$), and the annealing schedule parameter ($s(t)$).
main_assumptions: The analysis compares ideal Parity-QA vs. hardware-motivated decompositions, and assumes that single-qubit rotations are sufficient for ground state preparation in certain regimes.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the Ising ring structure in both logical and parity qubit representations, detailing the required multi-qubit gate transformations.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the frustrated Ising ring model, details the Parity Mapping technique to transform the Hamiltonian, and then analyzes its impact separately on continuous-time Quantum Annealing (QA) and the discrete QAOA protocol, concluding with complexity comparisons.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete algorithmic improvement for quantum computation by showing how mapping constraints can stabilize spectral gaps and reduce scaling in variational quantum algorithms applied to physically relevant models like frustrated magnets.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: The Ising ring with N = 7 in its logical representation (a) and parity representations (c)–(d). The parity transformation table is given in (b). Without ancillas the parity graph has an N-body constraint visualized by a grey polygon in (c). With ancilla interactions (red and blue dashed lines in (a)) the parity graph has three constraints of size three or four, shown in (d). The digital implementations of the multi-qubit gates are shown in (e), (f) and (g) for the logical graph, parity graph and the parity graph with ancillas, respectively.

FIG. 2: The frustrated Ising ring with N spins. The antiferromagnetic bond −Jf sits at site j = N; the two weak bonds Jw and J′ w flank the central spin at j = (N + 1)/2, with J′ w = Jw in the standard symmetric case. All remaining bonds equal J in the standard model and may take distinct values in the modified instances (see text). The dashed blue line indicates the possible reflection symmetry axis.

FIG. 3: Minimal energy gap ∆min versus system size N in the standard and parity implementations, for (a) the frustrated ring model (constraint strength C = J; note the logarithmic scale) and (b) the ring with uniform coupling magnitudes and a single antiferromagnetic bond (constraint strength C = 2J; linear scale). In both panels, solid coloured lines show the parity gap at fixed ancilla number na = 0, 1, . . . , 5, each starting at the smallest admissible ring N = 2na + 3; the grey dotted line is the realistic parity gap at the hardware-required na = (N −3)/2. In (a), the standard and realistic-parity gaps close as ∼e−0.96 N and ∼e−0.51 N, so the parity mapping roughly halves the decay...

FIG. 4: Ground state infidelity 1 −PGS vs circuit depth P (only single qubit z- and x-rotations) for the original formulation of the frustrated ring model and its adaptations for N = 7. The greater the number of distinct Jj values, the more layers P are needed to reach the ground state.

FIG. 5: The probability of being in the exact ground state PGS (upper plot) and the probability of a single physical qubit being in the up state P↑(lower plot) as a function of the single control parameter θz at fixed θx = π/4 (a single QAOA layer, P = 1). In the upper plot we show comparisons between N = 5 and N = 51. In the lower plot we show comparisons of qubits associated with different parameters ˜Jk = 1.0, 0.5 and −0.45.
